Good afternoon, colleagues. The 21st plenary meeting of the 11th emergency special session of the General Assembly is called to order. The Assembly will continue its consideration of agenda item 5, entitled "Letter dated 28 February 2014 from the Permanent Representative of Ukraine to the United Nations addressed to the President of the Security Council." I give the floor now to the distinguished representative of Czechia, His Excellency Eduard Holius, Deputy Minister for Foreign Affairs of Czechia.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, Three years ago, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a sovereign and independent nation. But let us not forget that this war commenced already 11 years ago, in February 2014, with the Russian occupation of Crimea and parts of Donbas. as part of a well-orchestrated expansionist plan to seize territories of a sovereign nation through aggression and to recreate neocolonial spheres of influence. The toll of this unprovoked war is disastrous. Millions of Ukrainians have been displaced. Thousands have been killed or injured. Powerful missiles and bombs systematically strike populated areas in Ukrainian cities, including schools, hospitals, and ports far away from the front line. Attacks against Ukraine's energy grid in the midst of winter have become one of the defining, abhorrent hallmarks of this war. With its deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure, Moscow cynically seeks to undermine the resilience of the Ukrainian men and women who, with remarkable courage, defend their country. And Russia's flagrant violation of international law doesn't stop there. Russia is responsible for a whole array of war crimes, violations of human rights and international humanitarian law in Ukraine. The United Nations investigation documented numerous cases of summary executions, torture, rape and other acts of violence used as Russia's tactic of war against Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war, as well as forced transfers and deportations of Ukrainian children. Czechia considers accountability as a cornerstone of any lasting peace. The leadership crime of aggression must not go unpunished, and those responsible for war crimes and other atrocities must be brought to justice. Otherwise, impunity will continue and widen. The invasion of Ukraine has also highlighted the stark link between aggression abroad and intensified repression of civil and political rights within Russia itself. One year after the death of Alexei Navalny, Russia continues its systemic crackdown on human rights, civil society, independent media, and dissent of any kind. Mr. President, this hall has heard repeated call of the international community on Russia to immediately cease hostilities, withdraw all its forces from Ukrainian territory, and respect Ukraine's independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders. A call that Russia, a permanent member of the Security Council, has chosen to ignore. Let me be clear. Until Russia respects the fundamental principles of international law, there can be no business as usual with the aggressor. Mr. President, in a year that many wait with hope, we reaffirm our unwavering commitment to a just and lasting peace in Ukraine. We all want to see this year as the year during which negotiated settlement based on international law is found. However, let me stress that no durable settlement for Ukraine can be found without Ukraine's participation and consent. Our own Czech history suggests that aggressors are seldom satisfied with concessions designed to appease them. Weak compromises embolden them and bring us nothing but more war and destruction. And Russia's imperialist aggression cannot be appeased. It must be faced with strength and resolve. Mr. President, we all have a stake in Ukraine prevailing as a sovereign nation within its internationally recognized borders. Czechia has fully supported the draft resolution A/ES/11/L.10 but put forward to our consideration by Ukraine, and stands firmly in solidarity with Ukraine and its people in their self-defence until a just and lasting peace in line with the United Nations Charter is finally secured. Thank you for your attention.

I thank the distinguished representative of Czechia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Georgia, His Excellency Lasha Darsalia, Deputy Minister for Foreign Affairs of Georgia.

Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies. The resumption of this emergency special session once again reminds us that the founding principles of this organization remain as relevant as ever. Every single day of the past three years, in the wake of Russia's war against Ukraine, has brought unbearable human harm and immense scale of destruction. The implication of this war has resonated far beyond the borders of one single member state and posed threat to international peace and security, further exacerbating global challenges. Excellencies. I would like to emphasize that Georgia's support for the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders is unwavering. Since the outbreak of the war, Georgia has demonstrated full solidarity with Ukraine through strong diplomatic steps, as well as by offering active and substantial humanitarian assistance. Georgia sponsored, joined, or supported around 600 documents and initiatives in major international organizations which, among others, included creation of special mechanisms in support of Ukraine. The government of Georgia has also been providing substantial humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since the beginning of the aggression. Georgia provided substantial humanitarian assistance to Ukraine, including the allocation of more than 1,000 tons of humanitarian aid, as well as financial assistance and extending support to Ukrainians arriving in Georgia. Georgia, as a responsible member of international community, believes that international diplomacy should play a crucial role in resolving conflicts by facilitating dialogue and cooperation among nations. More than 20 years have passed since Georgia regained its independence, albeit its past is still paved with the fight for sovereignty and territorial integrity. Our recent history, time and again, illustrates the crucial importance of peace and stability for further development. Only principled and proactive international engagement can help find the common ground and create a framework for effective resolution that is not achievable through confrontation. I'm confident that peaceful resolution of this war based on the charter and international law would promote regional stability in Europe by preventing further tensions and escalations. Distinguished delegates. Let me reaffirm once again Georgia's unwavering support to the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders, extending to its territorial waters. Georgia will stand in solidarity with Ukraine and the Ukrainian people on the path to comprehensive, lasting peace. Thank you very much.

I thank the distinguished representative of Georgia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Her Excellency Erika Schouten, Special Envoy for Ukraine of the Foreign Minister of the Kingdom of Netherlands.

Mr. President, distinguished delegates, the Netherlands aligns itself with the EU statement that will be delivered. Three years ago today, a line was crossed. Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity were violated. International law was trampled on. The very principles of the United Nations Charter were blatantly disregarded. Ukraine did not provoke this war, nor did it start it. Russia, a permanent member of the UN Security Council, a body with a special responsibility to uphold peace and security under the UN Charter, chose to violate Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and thereby the founding principles on which this Organization is built. Today's vote is a clear signal in support of international law, upholding the UN Charter and against creating a world where might is right. Ending the war with a quick fix gives the aggressor the opportunity for repetition and will set a precedent for aggressors elsewhere. For three years, the people of Ukraine have demonstrated extraordinary resilience against Russia's unprovoked aggression. But the costs have been staggering, at the front line and behind the front line, as Russia continues its attacks on energy and other civilian infrastructure, and on cultural objects, on a daily basis. And in the occupied territories, where, according to the Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, Russia's occupation brings widespread suffering and oppression. Russia intends to break the Ukrainian spirit, artificially alter its demographics, and forcibly Russify millions under occupation and destroy Ukrainian identity. We cannot let Russia succeed. Russia's aggression has had devastating and long-lasting consequences, also for the world as a whole. Food and energy prices have soared. The environment has been adversely affected. And there is an escalating risk of a nuclear disaster due to Russia's attacks on the Ukrainian power grid connected to the nuclear plants. We all want peace, the Ukrainian people most of all. And there will be peace the moment Russia stops the fighting. But it cannot be peace at any cost. Peace must be just, comprehensive and lasting. And Ukraine must have a seat at the negotiating table to decide on its future. Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine. A just peace also means that international crimes do not go unpunished, including the crime of aggression. To ensure might does not make right, we need to respect all principles we have vowed to uphold, now and in the future. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union.

President, colleagues. I have the honor to speak on behalf of the European Union and 26 member states. We gathered in this hall today to reiterate three full years since Russia launched its illegal and provoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine, our unwavering support for international law and for the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity enshrined in the UN Charter. We gathered today to advocate for an early end to the war of aggression and for a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace in Ukraine in line with the UN Charter. Those core principles are not abstract ideals. They are vital pillars for every nation within the UN. They apply to all of us. The foundation of a multilateral system is at risk if the UN core principles are undermined. and if we allow the power of guns to replace in our troubled world the power of law. It is that simple and that vital. We support all meaningful efforts under the UN Charter to bring an end to Russia's war of aggression. No one wants and needs peace in Ukraine more than the Ukrainian people. No one has a larger stake in European security than Europeans. And no one can afford to ignore the devastating consequences of this war for regional and global stability. Dear colleagues, the Ukraine resolution that we adopted today reiterates in the strongest way the UN membership's call for renewed diplomatic efforts towards a comprehensive, just and lasting peace, an early peace in Ukraine this year, in line with the UN Charter. We took every effort to ensure that the process to prepare this resolution, together with our Ukrainian colleagues, should be transparent and inclusive. Together with Ukraine, we spared no effort to take comments on board as much as possible. We are grateful to all delegations that engaged with us in this process. Your efforts strengthened the text that was adopted today. Thank you. Colleagues, the time for peace is now. And peace must be just, lasting, and comprehensive. Any peace that risks rewarding aggression increases the risk for any country, wherever in the world, to face similar aggression. It creates a dangerous precedent for the future, undermining the principles of international law and the sovereignty of all nations. But a peace that is in line with the core principles of the UN Charter ensures a safer world for all of us. And we believe that in today's turbulent world, It is especially imperative to ensure that our calls for peace leave absolutely no doubt about the UN membership's commitment to UN principles, the UN Charter, and the territorial integrity and sovereignty of nations. And this is exactly what we did today. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the European Union. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Switzerland.

Mr. President, developments in relation to Ukraine are currently evolving rapidly. While Switzerland is monitoring the situation closely, we see this day of commemoration as an opportunity to reaffirm the principles that unite us, in particular respect for international law, including the United Nations Charter. We remain steadfast in our support for Ukraine and call for an immediate end to hostilities We call on Russia to withdraw its troops from the entire territory of Ukraine. Above all, we place the Ukrainian people at the heart of our concerns. The human cost of this war is immense. It continues to cause indescribable loss and suffering, leaving millions in need of humanitarian aid or forcing them to flee their homes. More than half of Ukraine's energy facilities have been damaged or destroyed. We reiterate that a nuclear accident must be avoided at all costs. Switzerland emphasizes that the civilian population and infrastructure are protected by international humanitarian law and that attacks against them are prohibited. We call on all parties to the conflict to respect international humanitarian law in all circumstances. This also includes the obligation to authorize and facilitate rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access. We have stated this on several occasions. Beyond Ukraine, this war has profound consequences. It destabilizes food security and energy supply, as well as international security. This war, therefore, endangers future generations. Mr. President, Russia's military aggression against Ukraine constitutes a serious violation of international law, in particular of Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. It jeopardizes our multilateral order. as well as the very principles of the United Nations Charter, obligations that all of us, as Member States of this Organization, have pledged to respect. The resolution presented by Ukraine, which we have adopted today, carries a powerful message, a call for an end to the war, for diplomacy and for respect for international law. It advocates peace. True to this commitment, Switzerland is strongly involved, whether that be through our Security Council mandate, the organization of the Bergenstock Conference in June 2024, or its targeted aid for reconstruction and in the humanitarian field. We will continue to work to contribute to peace and security in Europe when we chair the OSCE in 2026. Above all, Switzerland remains firmly committed to a comprehensive, just and lasting peace for Ukraine based on international law, including the United Nations Charter. We welcome any initiative that could lead to the achievement of this goal. It is essential that Ukraine be involved in these discussions from the outset, as its future depends on it. As the General Assembly, it is our responsibility to recall and defend the principles that unite us. In this way, we can move towards a future in which peace will prevail for all of us. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Switzerland. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Bulgaria.

Today, we solemnly mark three years since the start of Russia's illegal, unprovoked, and utterly unjustified full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine. For three long years, the Ukrainian people have endured immense suffering, loss, and destruction as they bravely defend their homeland. Bulgaria strongly condemns Russia's ongoing war of aggression, which constitutes a blatant violation of international law, the UN Charter, and the fundamental principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity. This war is a direct challenge to the rules-based international order. We must ensure that military aggression and territorial annexation never become viable means of achieving geopolitical goals. We reaffirm our unwavering support for Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity with internationally recognized borders. Bulgaria calls for the immediate cessation of hostilities and the full withdrawal of Russian forces from Ukrainian territory. We urge Russia to engage in meaningful dialogue and diplomacy to reach a peaceful resolution in full accordance with the UN Charter and international law. Any discussion on peace must be firmly rooted in international law and the UN Charter. No peace initiative or negotiation framework should be pursued without Ukraine's direct involvement. Furthermore, Ukraine must enter any negotiations from the strongest possible position. The foundation of any future peace must include accountability for Russia's crimes in Ukraine. We emphasize the need to hold those responsible for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and other atrocities to account. We also recall the obligation of all states under Article 2 of the United Nations Charter. Bulgaria welcomes recent steps towards establishing a special tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine. We firmly believe that Ukraine's future lies within the European family at a transatlantic community, and we stand ready to support Ukraine on this path. Russia's war of aggression has also underscored the strategic importance of security and resilience in the Black Sea region, one of the most affected by this conflict. Stability and cooperation in the Black Sea must be addressed within the broader context of Euro-Atlantic security. In this regard, the swift adoption of the new EU Black Sea strategy, focusing on connectivity, stability, economic cooperation, and the resilience of neighboring countries, is of paramount importance. As we mark this grim anniversary, this Assembly has spoken in favour of a just and lasting peace, one based on the UN Charter and the principles of sovereign equality and territorial integrity of States. The path of peace begins where Russia's aggression against Ukraine ends. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Bulgaria. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Slovakia.

Mr. President, we fully align ourselves with the statement made by the representative of the European Union. And I can therefore be very brief. Slovakia has co-sponsored the resolution submitted by Ukraine and voted yes. Mr. President, three years ago, Russia invaded Ukraine in violation of the United Nations Charter and international law. The military invasion is still going on. The world recognizes the strength and bravery of Ukrainian people fighting for their survival. Let me reiterate that Slovakia supports the sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders as a matter of principle. Borders must be respected and cannot be changed by force. Mr. President, the physical devastation and the humanitarian and economic costs to Ukraine caused by the conflict have been immense. The longer this tragedy goes on, the worse it will be and the more the human suffering it will entail. Slovakia has been taking concrete action to provide humanitarian assistance to Ukraine and to help and support people fleeing Ukraine on its territory since the onset of the war in 2022. Mr. President, as you know, the position of my country has been that this conflict must be ended diplomatically at the negotiating table in dialogue with all interested parties. Slovakia has consistently supported all international efforts dedicated to pursuing peace negotiations, including the joint proposal from China and Brazil for mediating peace. And we therefore welcome the commitment of President Trump to ending the Russian-Ukrainian war. and to a lasting peace in Ukraine. Slovakia supported the resolution proposed by the United States delegation today because it is consistent with our view on the peaceful settlement of disputes as enshrined in the United Nations Charter. Mr. President, we hope that meaningful progress involving all parties, including Ukraine and the European Union, will soon be made, leading to a just, and lasting peace, and also allowing Ukraine to feel confident about its future security. Thank you very much for your attention.
I thank the distinguished representative of Slovakia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Austria.

Excellencies, Mr. President, Austria aligns itself with the statement of the European Union Ambassador. It has been three years since Russia's unprovoked, unjustified, and illegal full-scale aggression against its neighbor, Ukraine. It has been three years since Russia has violated one of the core principles of the UN Charter, a clear violation of international law. And it has been three years that we have stood in solidarity with Ukraine. To this day, Ukrainian men, women, and children continue to suffer from Russian attacks, attacks that are in clear violation of international humanitarian law. It is clear civilians shall not be the object of attacks. We therefore repeat our calls to the leadership of the Russian Federation to immediately cease its brutal war against Ukraine and withdraw its military forces. Excellencies, Austria doesn't provide weapons to Ukraine, but in addition to our common European Union contributions, we have provided bilaterally almost 300 million euros in financial and humanitarian aid to Ukraine since February 22. And almost 100,000 Ukrainians have found a second home in our country, Austria. This comes in addition to, and not instead of, our continued humanitarian assistance to crises all around the world, including in Africa and, of course, the Middle East. Mr. President, the Russian aggression against Ukraine is not a European problem. It is not a European problem. It is a matter of global concern. We have all felt the consequences, but of course, especially those living in the world's most vulnerable countries, from delayed food deliveries to rising energy prices and threats of nuclear incidents. In addition to our firm rejection of any threats with nuclear weapons, we remain particularly concerned about the risk of damages to Ukraine's nuclear infrastructure. The recent strikes against the Chernobyl nuclear power plant are alarming. Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions specifically prohibits attacks against installations containing dangerous forces. We urge all actors to respect international law in this regard and reiterate our full support for the efforts by the IAEA and Director General Rafael Grossi. So what remedies do we have as the international community? As a neutral state that is not part of any military alliance for Austria, Action within the United Nations is key. And when international law is blatantly violated, we continue to stand up for the rule of law and our UN Charter. This is what today's debate is for. And this is what we would expect if we were in Ukraine's shoes. And this is also why we voted yes for the resolution tabled by Ukraine, to show solidarity with the civilian population, to stand up against violations of international law and to call for a peaceful solution on the basis of the UN Charter and international law. Thank you to all of you who supported this resolution and also to all of those who made efforts in this direction. I know it's sometimes hard. Mr. President, no one wants peace more than the people of Ukraine and, of course, also the people of Austria. Austria, much like Secretary-General Guterres has said, supports peace efforts in this regard. We are always in favour of peace. At the same time, it must be a peace, a comprehensive, just and lasting peace, a peace that is achieved on the table with Ukraine present and a peace in line with the UN Charter. Let me be clear. As our Chancellor, Alexander Schellenberg, has said, no negotiations about Ukraine without Ukraine, and no decisions on European security without Europe. Today, we sent a strong signal that an unprovoked aggression against any country cannot be accepted by the international community. Today, we stood up for international law. Today, we voted yes to preserve our Charter. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Austria. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Germany.

Thank you, Mr. President. Germany aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union. Mr. President, three years ago, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine and started a war that shook the foundations of European and global security. Russia violated a guiding principle upon which the United Nations was founded, that we respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all Member States, large and small. Today, the General Assembly has made its position clear. Together, we once again have agreed on the urgent need for a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine, consistent with the Charter of the United Nations. We have called for an immediate cessation of the hostilities of Russia against Ukraine, and we joined the call for accountability for the most serious crimes committed on the territory of Ukraine. Russia must end its war of aggression. This war must end in line with our UN Charter, with full respect to the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders. And the war must end in a way that guarantees that Russia never again uses force to attempt to redraw the borders of Ukraine, violating Europe's security. A sham peace imposed against the will of the Ukrainian people will serve no one. The sovereignty of members of this organization must be protected. Every state must be able to freely choose its destiny without fearing aggression. That is why we have stood resolutely with Ukraine also today. And we will continue our support in solidarity with Ukraine in defense of Europe's security and for the sake of the UN Charter, the charter that safeguards all nations, large and small, from aggression. Mr. President, Excellencies, colleagues, the world is watching how we rise to the challenge of ending this war. Let us choose wisely. Let us choose justice. Let us choose a peace that ensures a safer world for all of us. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Germany. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom.

Mr. President, the United Kingdom welcomes the resumption of this special session on Ukraine. Three years on, Russia's illegal and unprovoked invasion has caused untold suffering, most recently in the massive wave of drone attacks over the weekend. reportedly the largest in a single night in three years. Millions of Ukrainians have fled their homes. Tens of thousands of civilians have been killed, children forcibly deported, schools, homes, hospitals, places of worship destroyed, and Russia's forces have committed the most appalling crimes: summary executions, torture, rape. Enough is enough, as the Secretary-General reminded us. And Russia's aggression did not begin three years ago, but long before that. When my Prime Minister spoke to President Zelensky this week, he was clear that any outcome to the war must safeguard Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. A peace that rewards aggression is not a real peace. And a peace that rewards aggression will not last, because Putin has a long track record of making deals with his fingers crossed behind his back. Well, not this time. We must not make the mistake of weak deals of the past. This time, there must be peace through strength. And that is why there can be no negotiation about Ukraine without Ukraine. Colleagues, it is not just Ukraine's security that is at stake. It is Britain's too. But it is the security of all of us, every single member state who does not want to see tanks driving over their border. killing their people, stealing their children, and redrawing their borders on a whim. Today, 93 countries again stood with Ukraine, voting to reaffirm our respect for Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and for the UN Charter. We all want an end to this war. No country more so than Ukraine and its people. As my Prime Minister has said, the UK is ready to play its part to support efforts for peace. And we will continue to support Ukraine to defend itself and to have its voice heard. But let us not forget a simple truth: that Russia could end this war tomorrow by ceasing its aggression and withdrawing its forces from Ukraine. But the Kremlin shows no more sign of that than they have done at any point in the last three years. So today, as for the last three years and for the future, we stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and with our allies for as long as it takes, until Ukraine wins a peace that respects the UN Charter and delivers a secure future for its people and for all of us. Thank you, President.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malta.

President, Today, as we gather to mark three years since Russia unleashed its war of aggression against Ukraine, we remember the countless civilians affected. Mothers and fathers, brothers and sisters, sons and daughters. Malta aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union. Today's gathering takes place at a very delicate time, with ongoing discussions on how to bring an end to this illegal and unjustified war. Diplomatic solutions, as underlined by the Secretary General, are the only way forward. Any talks must include the participation of Ukraine at all stages of negotiations if they are to lead to a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace, which ultimately safeguards the security interests of Ukraine and its people, in full respect of principles of sovereign equality and territorial integrity of states, as underlined in various UN resolutions. We continue to emphatically denounce Russia's decision to pursue aggression and inflict devastation. whilst commending the bravery, determination and resilience of Ukraine and its people, who continue to fight for freedom and the territorial integrity of Ukraine. We commend the unbreakable spirit and commitment to sovereignty, freedom and rule of law. The consequences of this war have been tragic, not only for Ukraine, but for global stability and order, putting considerable strain on our international rules-based order, putting in jeopardy international peace and security. Russia's unprovoked aggression against Ukraine has made us witness deliberate attacks against civilians, critical infrastructure, and energy systems, resulting in massive civilian casualties and human suffering. All these actions constitute serious violations of international law and international humanitarian law, for which Russia needs to be held accountable. Malta remains firm in calling on Russia to immediately cease all hostilities and to unconditionally and completely withdraw all its forces and military equipment from the entire territory of Ukraine within its internationally recognised borders. Malta also stands united with those who strive to uphold the universal principles enshrined in the United Nations Charter and to advance the implementation of the resolutions adopted by the General Assembly, including today. The sexual and gender-based violence in Ukraine and the forced deportations in Ukraine, notably relating to the transfers of children to Russia, remain a concern. We take this opportunity to call for the immediate cessation of such practices, with the safe return of all forcibly displaced individuals. In its documentation of war crimes, arbitrary detentions, as well as forced deportations, we continue to fully support the work of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine. We urge all parties to cooperate with this Commission and with other international mechanisms to ensure the accountability of such violations. President, accountability for all war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during this war of aggression is important not only to prevent impunity but also to bring justice to the victims. With the interest in safeguarding justice for victims, we remain firm in our commitment to ensure that all those responsible for international crimes are held accountable under international law. Represented as a beacon of hope and justice, we recall our steady support for the work of the International Criminal Court in its pursuit for lasting global peace. Likewise, we take this occasion to assert our backing for the establishment of a special tribunal with the aim of prosecuting crimes of aggression against Ukraine. President, the consequences of this war have likewise highlighted the necessity to continue stressing the importance of adhering to the indispensable pillars and concrete principles of ensuring nuclear safety, as well as security throughout the conflicts in Ukraine. We therefore reiterate our call on Russia to cease its relentless attacks upon Ukraine's critical energy infrastructure and to immediately withdraw all its occupying unauthorized military personnel from the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant. Given these circumstances, we've announced the latest attacks by Russia on the IAEA staff, as well as the Chernobyl nuclear power plant strikes, which raise new concerns vis-a-vis safety at nuclear facilities in Ukraine's conflict zones. Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine has not prevented countries around the world from providing humanitarian and other assistance to address needs in Ukraine. Malta has been active in providing humanitarian assistance to Ukraine, which we will continue to do so as long as it is necessary. We have also been proud to support humanitarian demining initiatives, which remain crucial to ensure sustainable reconstruction efforts in Ukraine. President, in closing, we believe that a just, lasting and comprehensive peace in Ukraine requires the immediate end of hostilities by Russia, together with the unconditional and full withdrawal of Russian military forces from Ukraine's entire territory in its internationally recognised borders. It is this spirit Malta will continue to support all efforts. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malta. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Albania.

Mr. President, three years ago, what started as a special military operation clearly was and continues to be an unprovoked and unjustified military aggression against Ukraine by a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council. By pursuing an expansionist agenda through force, Russia's war of choice has brought widespread devastation, causing immense civilian suffering, massive casualties, and the destruction of Ukraine's essential infrastructure. Mr. President, the full-scale invasion of Ukraine is in clear violation of the United Nations Charter and international law. The General Assembly has repeatedly condemned this aggression. The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants. The International Court of Justice has ordered the withdrawal of Russian forces from the Ukrainian territory. The United Nations has put Russian military forces and armed proxy groups in its list of shame over violations of children's rights in its war in Ukraine. In the face of this injustice, the Ukrainian people have demonstrated extraordinary courage defending their land and their freedom with unwavering resolve. Russia's initial ambitions have faltered, and the strength of Ukrainian spirit has proven far greater than Russia's military might. Colleagues, this aggression has not only devastated Ukraine, but has far-reaching consequences in our continent and beyond. It is our moral and legal obligation to condemn the breach of international law and the disrespect of UN Charter and stand by the people of Ukraine in their resistance to protect their own country. While this senseless war has lasted too long, it is time to put an end to it. We are increasingly optimistic that the recent efforts and engagement of the United States, together with the resolute support of the European Union, will provide the right impetus for achieving a just solution that will bring a durable peace for the region and Europe as a whole. The ultimate outcome of these concentrated efforts to end the war must be a just, sustainable, and comprehensive peace. One that fully upholds Ukraine's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity in accordance with the UN Charter, international law, and the resolutions of the General Assembly. Ukraine's future must be defined by its independence, its strength, and its prosperity, free to choose its own path without fear of further aggression. Moreover, we must ensure strong international guarantees that such violations and undermine of international law will never be tolerated. Accountability is not just an afterthought, it must be a central pillar of the peace process. In this context, Albania supports all efforts to achieve realistic and sustainable steps towards peace. A peace grounded in the principles of justice, sovereignty, and accountability. Mr. President, let me conclude by reaffirming Albania's unwavering support for Ukraine. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Albania. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Estonia.

President, today we mark three years since Russia launched an unprovoked and unjustified full-scale brutal war against Ukraine. This act of aggression is not only a vicious attack against an independent and sovereign Ukraine, but against the international law and the global peace, the UN Charter, global nonproliferation regime. Moreover, all this is having devastating effects to global food and energy markets in many parts of the world. Unfortunately, Russia's goals vis-a-vis Ukraine has not changed. To finish off Ukrainian nation and to erase sovereign Ukraine from the map, a plan which started back in 2014. I recall that Kremlin has repeatedly denied the legitimacy of the Ukrainian state, and its right to exist, and is increasingly desperate to remove democratically elected President Zelensky from power. War crimes, huge number of civilian deaths, grave human rights violations, thousands of deported Ukrainian children, total suffering and destruction that Russia has caused in Ukraine are a testament to those claims. Against all of the calls by member states and numerous UN General Assembly resolutions, Russia's aggression continues. According to the UN, in January this year alone, Russia's attacks caused almost 900 civilian casualties, including 21 children. Russia has continued shelling schools and hospitals, energy and food infrastructure. And on top of this, in February, struck with a war drone the Chernobyl nuclear power plant, in grave violation of International Atomic Energy Agency's seven indispensable pillars. Russia's aggression is economically, politically, and militarily supported by Iran, DPRK, and Belarus. Since last October, the DPRK has elevated its support by deploying troops to fight alongside Russian troops. This constitutes a major escalation, also indicating that Russia is suffering heavy casualties at the front lines and is struggling to recruit fresh cannon fodder. And indeed, it has been estimated that at current pace, Russia couldn't occupy the whole territory of Ukraine until the year 2075. And even this would be unattainable goal, as the number of Russian soldiers left to rot in the black Ukrainian soil is growing every single day. President, the resolution adopted today by the vast majority of the UN member states in the General Assembly calls for a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine based on accountability, principles of the UN Charter and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders, extending to its territorial waters. I hope that the Security Council would be able to follow the example of the most democratic and authoritative body of the UN, this General Assembly. Today, Estonia celebrates the 107th anniversary of our independence. were now only too well what losing freedom and independence means. The World War II ended with a peace deal that left Estonia and many other countries in Europe deprived of their independence and sovereignty and endured half a century of totalitarian Soviet oppression. This was not a just peace deal at all for us. To avoid the mistakes of the past, We should not try to appease the criminal on the ICC wanted list and neglect their accountability for the crime of aggression, as this would only lead to new crimes and more bloodshed. Appeased dictators will always come back for more. How to achieve just and lasting peace? Yulia Navalnaya, widow of the leading Russian opposition figure Alexei Navalny, who was starved and then killed by Kremlin in Siberian Gulag, recently warned, I quote, "There is no point to negotiate with Putin. He will lie, he will betray. If he remains in power, he will find a way to break the agreement. If he loses power, the agreement will become meaningless." End of quote. So the question really is, how can one trust somebody who cheats and changes the rules of a game under the guise of new realities, whenever suitable or beneficial? What is Putin's legitimacy worth after 25 years of clinging to power? which have included regular and massive election fraud, physical elimination of political opponents, extensive violations of human rights, war crimes, and extrajudicial killings, including the use of chemical weapons. Only free and fair elections, which the Russian people can only dream about for the last decades, would erode the real support for the dictator. It is quite clear his ratings are not even close to what Kremlin's propaganda honks. It appears also relevant to repeat again loud and clear that when it comes to a so-called root causes of this war, it is Russia's imperial and neocolonial obsession with Ukraine and denial of Ukraine's existence that unleashed its aggression. The root cause of the war in Ukraine is Putin unwillingness to accept the irreversibility of the collapse of the Soviet Union. So let's not succumb to Russian propaganda. Russia is still an aggressor and Ukraine is still the victim of the aggression. The Member States who supported the resolution on just and lasting peace in Ukraine thereby supported the UN Charter, the international law, and rejected spheres of influence and might makes right conduct in international relations. I want to thank you all for this. I want to thank you all for this. Together, we need to uphold the principles of the UN Charter more than ever. We all need a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace, not just a shady deal at the expense of Ukraine and the UN Charter. It is obvious that achieving just and lasting peace in Ukraine without Europe and Ukraine participating in the negotiations over the European security architecture is an illusion, and a dangerous one. In conclusion, let me once again insist that Russia immediately, completely, and unconditionally withdraws its military forces and mercenaries from the entire territory of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders. This would be the quickest way to peace. Until then, let me assure that Estonia is determined to continue supporting Ukraine by all means at our disposal. Supporting Ukraine's right for self-defense, according to Article 51 of the UN Charter, is the right thing to do from the moral, legal, and global security point of view. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Estonia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Republic of Moldova.

Mr. President, honorable ministers, excellencies, distinguished delegates, it has been three years already since Russia's full-scale and relentless war of aggression against Ukraine triggered unimaginable suffering and destruction with far-reaching implications for international peace and security. We resolutely condemn this brutal war and reaffirm our unwavering support for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders, including its territorial waters. The ongoing conflict continues to devastate civilians' lives and infrastructure, causing large-scale displacement and destruction. According to the data published by UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, at least 139 civilians were killed and 738 injured in Ukraine in January 2025. This means 39% increase from December 24 and 27% higher than casualties in January 24. Moreover, As per the information released by Office of High Commissioner for Humanitarian Assistance, in 2025, 12.7 million people, representing 36% of the Ukrainian population, require humanitarian assistance. The figures just mentioned are staggering. An act of aggression is persisting on a sovereign country in total disregard of the principles of the United Nations Charter and the international law. We recall the obligation of the states under Article 2 of the United Nations Charter to refrain in their international relations from the threat of use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. All the attacks on civilians and civilians infrastructure constitute violations of international law and humanitarian law, and we call on Russian Federation to stop those attacks immediately. Accountability is key for the prevention of atrocities and essential for providing a measure of justice to victims of this war. We reiterate our full support for the work of the United Nations to monitor and report on human rights violations and abuse, and to sustain accountability efforts. Furthermore, we support the endeavor by the international community to set up a special tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine. Mr. President. The Republic of Moldova is also greatly impacted by Russia's unprovoked aggression. While Ukraine is resisting a military invasion, my country is on the front line of a hybrid war, which includes interalia gas blackmail, cyberattacks, sabotage, disinformation, and more. Our airspace has been violated several times by Russia's missiles and missile debris landed on our territory. The most recent incident in this regard being registered on 13th of February. The Republic of Moldova firmly condemns such violations, which represent a breach of our sovereignty and a serious threat to our national security. We are committed to further countering these risks in a systematic, legal, and peaceful manner. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, the Republic of Moldova is proud to be one of the cosponsors of the draft resolution adopted today by this esteemed Assembly on advancing peace in Ukraine. This document establishes essential guidelines for achieving a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine. We remain steadfast in our commitment to upholding the principles of international law and ensuring respect for Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. The resolution rightly underscores the necessity of fully implementing the relevant General Assembly resolution adopted in response to the aggression against Ukraine. In particular, we reiterate the urgent demand for Russian Federation to immediately, completely, and unconditionally withdraw all its military forces from the territory of Ukraine within the internationally recognized borders, a fundamental requisite for lasting and sustainable resolution of this war. We urge the international community to remain resolute in the face of Russia's unprovoked aggression and to support the efforts towards a comprehensive, sustainable, and lasting peace. Only a just resolution, one that ensures accountability and prevents future aggression, can bring justice to victims of this war and lay the foundation for long-term security in the region. In closing, Mr. President, the Republic of Moldova reaffirms its unwavering solidarity with Ukraine and Ukrainian people in this unjustified war of aggression, and people who are courageously defending their territory and striving for a just peace, a peace that would respect Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity in line with the provisions of the United Nations Charter, international law, and the relevant General Assembly resolutions. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Republic of Moldova. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Portugal.

Mr. President, Portugal stands here today with Ukraine. We align with the EU statement and we are very pleased with the adoption of the resolution on advancing a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine, which highlights the commitment of this General Assembly to the UN Charter and to international law. We have also supported the adoption of the resolution on the path to peace, as amended. We all want peace. Portugal is unarguably in favour of peace, just not any peace. Mr. President, 80 years ago, representatives of the international community took upon themselves the duty to work together to maintain international peace and security and to prevent future generations from experiencing war. They did so by writing a legally binding document that has shaped our common history for the last eight decades. and has established a rules-based multilateral order with the United Nations at its core. We are looking forward to commemorating these major mankind's achievements throughout this year. However, today, we are sadly here to evoke the third anniversary of a breach to this contract. Indeed, three years ago, Russia, a permanent member of the Security Council, has violated its provisions by starting a war in Europe that has caused the suffering of thousands of people and has unleashed a worldwide political and economic turmoil. With the adoption of today's resolution, we once again condemn such violation of the territorial integrity of a sovereign country and, above all, call for a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine, in full compliance of the UN Charter, international law and this Assembly's resolution. We supported this resolution in line with Portugal's unwavering support for international law and for the principles of sovereignty and territorial independence, sovereignty and the territorial integrity without ambiguities and in all geographies, in Europe, but also in Africa and in the Middle East, while also reaffirming our joint commitment to the protection of civilians from the atrocities of war. By calling for a peaceful resolution of the war against Ukraine, we commend all meaningful diplomatic endeavors that support Ukraine in its efforts to achieve a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace. With our European partners, we are ready to contribute to any negotiations that ensure the sustainability of a peace process. that the reconstruction of the country and its future prosperity, stability, and independence. In concluding, Mr. President, by standing with Ukraine throughout its path to peace and freedom, the international community reaffirms its longstanding pledge to the key principles of the UN Charter as we approach the 80th milestone of our common, invaluable history of the UN. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Portugal. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Vietnam.

Mr. President, three years ago.

This very podium, my delegation affirmed that once they erupt, wars and conflicts only inflict immense suffering to human beings and grave consequences for many others. To this day, the loss of human lives and devastation resulting from the conflict in Ukraine are immeasurable. The negative impact and destabilizing effects extend beyond those directly involved, casting broader regional and global implications. Vietnam follows closely the situation in Ukraine and the far-reaching impacts of the conflict with a heavy heart. Having borne the heavy toll of wars, our nation deeply understands the scars of conflicts and the value of peace. Vietnam continues to call for an immediate end to violence, hostilities, and any actions that fuel further escalation. Our priority is safeguarding the security of civilians, protecting critical civilian infrastructure, and addressing the urgent humanitarian needs of those affected by the conflict. Vietnam's consistent stance from day one of the conflict and even beyond is broke out has remained that all disputes must be resolved through peaceful means and the fundamental principles of international law and the UN Charter must be upheld. This include respecting the independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity of states and refraining from the threat of use of force. We regret that many opportunities for peace have been missed in the past three years. This conflict needs to come to an end. The human suffering must end. Today marks a critical juncture. for us to work together and contribute to peace in Ukraine. It is all the more crucial for the UN membership to promote actions that foster consensus, inclusivity, and with the active participation and concurrence of all directly involved parties, instead of division and confrontation. This will pave the way for a lasting comprehensive and acceptable solution to all to resolve this conflict. And such a solution can only be achieved through peaceful means in adherence to international law and the UN Charter, and taking into account the legitimate interest and the role of all parties concerned for the stability and security of the region and the world. Vietnam commends and supports all constructive initiatives, including of the UN, in this direction. For our part, Vietnam stands ready to make our contributions to diplomatic efforts and to the reconstruction, recovery and assistance in Ukraine. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Vietnam. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Italy.

Mr. President, Italy fully aligns itself with the statement by the European Union and would like to add some considerations in its national capacity. On the third tragic anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, we stand together with the Ukrainian people to reaffirm our unwavering commitment to our shared values and the UN Charter. The 11th Emergency Special Session of the General Assembly is convened today to reaffirm the need to ensure that the fundamental principles of international law prevail. not just in Ukraine, but wherever they are challenged. Italy remains committed to a comprehensive, just and lasting peace based on the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of Ukraine. We firmly believe that the full implementation of these principles is not only in the interest of Ukraine and Europe, but also of the entire UN membership, since they are the foundations that hold the international community together. We are not at war with Russia, but we defend Ukraine's right to be an independent state. We must work together to restore peace in Europe.

We need diplomacy.

There is no military solution to this conflict, but only diplomatic, to be achieved through negotiations. And we appreciate the U.S. diplomatic initiative aimed at bringing Russia to the negotiating table. For that reason, we decided to support both resolutions, advanced a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and the path to peace as amended. At the same time, we believe that only the full involvement of Ukraine and Europe in these negotiations can guarantee a lasting peace in line with the Charter of the United Nations. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Italy. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Luxembourg.

President, Luxembourg aligns itself fully with the statement from the European Union. Allow me to add a few considerations in our national capacity. Three years ago to the day, Russia launched a large-scale war of aggression against its neighbor, Ukraine, a sovereign member state of our organization. While we meet here today, Russian forces are continuing their attacks against civilian people and infrastructure in Ukraine in violation of international humanitarian law. It is therefore more urgent than ever that the General Assembly stand in favour of a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine. That was the objective of the first resolution that we adopted this morning. Luxembourg is proud to have co-sponsored and voted in favour of this resolution, prepared by Ukraine with the support of the European Union. The resolution took into account suggestions made throughout the inclusive and transparent consultations that took place. We'd like to thank all Member States who voted in favour of this resolution. It is in everyone's interest to defend the United Nations Charter and to this year achieve comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine. This resolution recalls a demand on Russia to withdraw all its military forces from Ukraine's territory, while calling for a cessation of hostilities as soon as possible. In voting in favour of this text, we demonstrated our solidarity with the Ukrainian people and our determination to ensure that international law is respected and prevails. Luxembourg also voted in favour of the resolution prepared by the United States entitled "A path to peace". We voted in favour of this following the inclusion of three essential amendments on the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine and just peace in Ukraine in line with the United Nations Charter. It's important to recall who the aggressor is. It was Russia that launched a large-scale invasion of Ukraine three years ago. In launching its large-scale aggression, an aggression that was unprovoked, unjustified and unjustifiable against Ukraine, on the 24th of February 2022, Russia not only attacked Ukraine, Russia also flouted the international rule of law-based order, which is underpinned by the United Nations Charter, and in doing so, it threatened security and stability around the world. There is the Numbers of this war of aggression are terrifying. Hundreds of thousands of people have lost their lives. Men, women, and children have been victim of abject violence, including sexual violence. This war has destroyed infrastructure, education infrastructure, health infrastructure, and energy too. It has also left deep-rooted psychological scars on the Ukrainian people. Ukraine today has the most mines in the world. A third of its territory is covered with mines and unexploded ordnance. This situation is a major challenge for long-term security and reconstruction of the country. That's why our support to Ukraine includes humanitarian demining. The resolution submitted by Ukraine that we adopted this morning also underscores the need to ensure that the perpetrators of the gravest crimes under international law that have been committed on Ukrainian territory be brought to justice and that justice be served for the victims, also to prevent future crimes. In this context, Luxembourg welcomes the role played by the International Criminal Court, which has already issued several arrest warrants. As the ICC cannot try the crime of aggression in this particular case, we support the creation of a special tribunal for crime of aggression against Ukraine. President, efforts to put an end to the war via diplomacy and dialogue are welcome, in as much as these efforts are also underpinned by the principles of the United Nations Charter. Peace in Ukraine will only last if it is a just peace backed up by solid and reliable security guarantees. Peace and security and peace in Ukraine and Europe security are indissociable. Peace in Ukraine will only last if Ukraine and the European Union are fully involved in negotiations. Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine, nothing about Europe without Europe. In its brave fight to defend its freedom and universal values, Ukraine can continue to count on the full support and solidarity of Luxembourg. Luxembourg will continue to resolutely support the independence, unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognised borders. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Luxembourg. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Slovenia.

Thank you, Mr. President. At the outset, I would like to welcome the successful adoption of the resolution this morning. The overwhelming support it received reflects the international community's support of Ukraine, its commitment to the integrity of the UN Charter, and the principles of territorial integrity and settling of disputes by peaceful means. Mr. President, three years have passed since Russia started its unprovoked and illegal aggression against Ukraine, in blatant violation of international law. For three years, we have been witnessing Russia's systematic destruction of Ukraine's civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, schools, residential buildings, and energy grids, and a campaign of oppression of its citizens. Three years of war have produced immense destruction and widespread damage to essential and civilian infrastructure. Deliberate attacks against the Ukrainian energy infrastructure have caused a severe energy shortfall. Some 10% of Ukraine's homes are estimated to have been damaged or destroyed. More than 800 hospitals were damaged and over 370 schools were destroyed. Three years of war also amounted to immense human suffering. The toll on civilian lives is unbearable. Reports also show that every second Ukrainian citizen has been chronically affected by the war. Nearly two-thirds of households are dealing with mental health challenges of their family members. and hundreds of thousands of children are experiencing or are at risk of developing a post-traumatic stress disorder. The intense fighting has displaced over 6.9 million people, and almost 13 million civilians are left in need of humanitarian assistance. This is enough suffering and destruction for a lifetime, and it needs to stop now. Each day this war continues, international humanitarian law is disregarded, violated, and undermined. With each day, the integrity of the UN Charter is ever more at risk. Mr. President, we all want to see peace in Ukraine as soon as possible. But it matters greatly how the peace process ends. Russian aggression must stop. Ceasefire must be achieved and sufficient security guarantees for Ukraine ensured. Negotiations for just and lasting peace must be held with Ukraine and the European Union at the negotiating table. Any peace talks must be anchored in the principles that we have agreed to in the UN Charter, including the respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity of its member states. Slovenia is ready to support the endeavors to reach a just and lasting peace in line with the UN Charter. which will aim to rebuild trust and bring about lasting peace and stability in Eastern Europe. A just and lasting peace also calls for accountability. Slovenia will therefore, in the General Assembly and elsewhere, continue to scrutinize the implementation of international law, particularly international humanitarian law and human rights law. We will continue to call for accountability for international crimes including war crimes and crimes against humanity. Mr. President, lasting peace is not just the absence of war, but also the presence of justice, accountability, and the unwavering respect for international law. Slovenia stands ready to support such efforts to end the war in Ukraine, bringing a long overdue peace to the Ukrainian people. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Slovenia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Liechtenstein.

Mr. President, today we commemorate once again Russia's aggression against Ukraine that, as we often tend to forget, had its inception in February 2014 with the invasion of eastern Ukraine and the attempted illegal annexation of Crimea. On this very day three years ago, Russia launched its full-scale invasion against its neighbor in blatant violation of the UN Charter, causing immense suffering for the people of Ukraine, but also impacting the entire world. The drone attack against the Chernobyl nuclear power plant two weeks ago and Russia's deployment of troops from the DPRK are just recent examples that demonstrate clearly the regional and global ramifications of this illegal war waged by Russia, and that it must be of continuous concern to all of us committed to the UN Charter and the international rule of law. In retrospect, it is clear that our response to the aggression of 2014 was insufficient. GA resolution 68/262 lacked the necessary clarity and determination to unequivocally condemn the aggression by the Russian Federation and even failed to identify it as such. This limited response, far from preventing subsequent acts of aggression, has de facto been a contributing factor to Russia's full-scale invasion three years ago. We must acknowledge the shortcomings of our collective action and recognize the need to respond to future cases with greater resolve from the outset. It is our collective responsibility to uphold the purposes and principles of the UN Charter. Mr. President, the resolutions adopted by this Assembly in the framework of the 11th Emergency Special Session since 2022 demonstrate a more robust and principled approach. By adopting two resolutions today on advancing a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine and on the path to peace with the strong majority of the membership of this organization, this Assembly has again demonstrated its ability to play its role in matters of peace and security and reiterated the relevant parameters for a just and lasting peace in Ukraine. The implementation of these resolutions is key, especially to bring an end to the continuous fighting that has caused immense suffering to the civilian population, to ensure accountability for the crimes committed under international law, including the crime of aggression, and to bring justice for all victims and survivors. Meaningful initiatives for a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine must be based on the UN Charter, in particular the principles of sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity, international law, and relevant GA resolutions. They need to include all relevant parties, and especially Ukraine, the victim state of aggression, who indeed has signaled its willingness to engage in peace talks. as well as those involved in the execution of a peace agreement, one that not only brings just and lasting peace to Ukraine, but also security to the entire region. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Liechtenstein. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela.

Mr. President, as a founding member of the United Nations, the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela is a firm defender of the purposes and principles enshrined in the foundational charter of our organization, as well as the norms of international law. Mr. President, When addressing the issue of Ukraine, my country, faithful as we are to our diplomacy for peace, has always opted for the peaceful settlement of the conflict. With this spirit in mind, we supported in the Security Council in 2015 the package of measures for the implementation of the Minsk agreements. This year, we saw a diplomatic path built towards achieving a solution to the civil war in Ukraine. Unfortunately, these agreements were used as an excuse to gain time and to further increase armed force leading to greater national division. In 2022, a new phase of the conflict was seen with the outbreak of an internal civil war and then a confrontation, international confrontation between Ukraine and the Russian Federation. At that time, we avoided joining the warmongering propaganda which called for reigniting the conflict and we decisively supported peace negotiations that began in Belarus and then continued in Turkey. These negotiations were very close to achieving a solution to the conflict. But today we know that they were interrupted by very influential actors from third states interested in continuing and expanding the war. Today, after hundreds of thousands of people have been killed on the battlefield and after millions of innocent civilians have had their lives ruined and become displaced, and the massive destruction of the economic infrastructure of the two countries, the conflict runs the risk of expanding once again into a third phase that will be more dangerous and even more destructive. A group of countries is convinced that they can expand their presence within Ukraine by accelerating the arms race and imposing a military solution to the conflict. the last months of 2024 we saw the transfer to this third level where nuclear powers are ever increasingly involved in Ukraine with arms technology and training of troops all of this running the risk of unleashing a global conflict this is the path of the growing war that we have seen since 2015 given the alternative to endless war. In recent weeks, there has been a new proposal for negotiation to achieve sustainable and permanent peace at the three levels of the conflict. We are now facing a fork in the road. Do we continue with the war, or do we achieve peace through dialogue, diplomacy, and political negotiation? The United Nations was born after the worst war in history in order to guarantee international peace and security, its greatest success has been to avoid a third world war. Also, when it has not been possible to avoid an armed conflict, the role of our Organization has been, through political negotiation, to steer conflicts towards the path of diplomacy for their peaceful resolution. This is our obligation today to correct the course and to build a path which prevents an escalation of tension. For these reasons, we welcome the initiative proposed today to the General Assembly entitled A Path to Peace. because, on the basis of practical and realistic arrangements, it attempts to put an end to the conflict in Ukraine through dialogue. We call upon the responsible members of the international community to give an opportunity for these negotiations to begin in order to provide a comprehensive and lasting solution that will benefit the peoples of Ukraine and the Russian Federation. Our role, Mr. President, is not to feed tensions and divisions. We need to put an end to any action that would tend to create greater confrontation, dividing the world into blocks, promoting hateful ideologies, using incendiary rhetoric and war-mongering propaganda to justify the provision of arms, which simply extends wars, and also the imposition of unilateral coercive measures, which will never lead to lasting peace. The last three years of the war have shown clearly that this is the path to destruction. For these reasons, we believe that the draft resolution contained in document A/ES.11/L.10, and recently adopted, well, adopted today by this General Assembly, contains selectivity which does not help to create the conditions necessary for moving towards peace between Russian Federation and Ukraine. Likewise, the amendments proposed in L13, L14 and L15 seem to want to remove all content from the offer for a rapid end to the conflict and achieving lasting peace, as was clearly proposed in the original version of the draft resolution A Path to Peace. Mr. President, to conclude. In Venezuela, we recognize that initiatives for peace dialogues, such as that presented today to the General Assembly, are more than unusual. They are really extraordinary. The selfish political calculations or the differences that we want to maintain with other states should not close the doors to this singular opportunity to put an end to a longstanding war that will continue to expand without end. we must comply with the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and defend the right to peace of the peoples of Ukraine and the Russian Federation. Thank you very much, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Australia.

Thank you, Mr. President. For three years, Australia has stood with Ukraine as it bravely defends itself from Russia's illegal and immoral full-scale invasion in flagrant violation of the UN Charter. As a permanent member of the UN Security Council, Russia has an obligation to uphold international peace and security. yet it has chosen to target the sovereignty and territorial integrity of its peaceful neighbor. Russia's actions, including its destruction of Ukraine's agricultural land and export infrastructure, cause harm globally, including for countries already facing acute food and energy insecurity, raising the cost of living for people all over the world. Australia believes that all countries are better off in a world where differences and disputes are settled through institutions, agreed rules and norms, and not by power and size alone. The fate of Ukraine is a test for these international rules that have underpinned global peace, stability and prosperity. North Korea's deployment of thousands of troops to aid Russia is a dangerous escalation of the war. Deepening military cooperation between Russia and North Korea is destabilising Europe and threatening the security of Australia's region, the Indo-Pacific. Australia also has deep concerns regarding dual-use goods trade that sustains Russia's military. We urge all countries, including China, to step up efforts to prevent this trade which supports Russia's invasion and defence industrial base. Russia's war has been marked by numerous reports of war crimes and human rights violations. Russia must adhere to its obligations under international humanitarian law, including the protection of civilians, including aid workers, and the treatment of civilian detainees and prisoners of war. Russia must provide full access to the International Committee of the Red Cross to all areas of Ukraine temporarily controlled by Russia, including all places of detention. Australia unreservedly condemns Russia's irresponsible nuclear rhetoric and saber-rattling through its illegal invasion. Despite condemnation from a majority of UN member states in July 2024, Russia's war has increased the risk of a catastrophic nuclear accident. Continued attacks on infrastructure and reckless conduct threatens to compromise nuclear safety, particularly at Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia and Chernobyl nuclear power plants. President, we welcome all meaningful progress towards a just and sustainable peace. A lasting peace should uphold Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity, support security and stability in Europe, and ensure Russia does not renew its aggression. For any peace deal to succeed, negotiations must include Ukraine. Australia is providing meaningful support totalling over $1.5 billion in military, economic, humanitarian and energy support to Ukraine. And we have implemented a comprehensive suite of economic measures to ensure Australia does not fund Russia's aggression. On this sombre milestone, Australia mourns Ukraine's losses and reflects on the bravery and resilience of the Ukrainian people. The international community must come together to advance and achieve a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Australia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Japan.

Thank you, Mr. President. It is with great sadness and pain that we are in this emergency special session, marking three years since Russia began its unprovoked war of aggression against the sovereign nation of Ukraine. This war, which has caused innumerable tragedies over the past three years, should have ended earlier. Japan appreciates all the diplomatic efforts concerning the situation in Ukraine and once again emphasizes the importance of solidarity on our side in the pursuit for peace in the country. During this period, many innocent civilians have lost their lives, and many more have been injured by Russia's ruthless and indiscriminate attacks on critical infrastructure, including hospitals, schools, and power plants. The effects of Russia's aggression also have global repercussions in such far-reaching areas as food security, energy, finance, the environment, and nuclear security and safety. Japan reaffirms its respect and solidarity with the people of Ukraine, who have demonstrated remarkable resilience in defending their country and its future over the past three years. Mr. President, In a world of diverse views and positions, the UN Charter serves as a foundation of all international relations and a common agreement that Member States must faithfully observe. Russia's aggression against Ukraine is, however, a clear and blatant violation of international law, including the UN Charter, as this General Assembly has repeatedly stated, and an act that fundamentally undermines the foundation. If such violations were tolerated, it would set a dangerous precedent, returning us to a jungle dominated by brute force and coercion. For this very reason, it is imperative we stand side by side with the people of Ukraine. Japan condemns in its strongest terms Russia's aggression against Ukraine and strongly demands that Russia cease its aggression immediately and listen to the voice of the international community. In this regard, we appreciate the various diplomatic efforts which are currently ongoing, including those of the United States, and hope that those efforts lead a breakthrough in the situation. Mr. President, Japan also strongly condemns the engagement of North Korea's troops in combat against Ukraine, which also constitutes a clear violation of international law, including the UN Charter. This unlawful, unjustified, and unacceptable military cooperation between Russia and the DPRK has expanded the scope of the conflict beyond the region and undermines global peace and security. Furthermore, Japan reiterates its deep concern about the military cooperation between Iran and Russia. The international community must refrain from any action, direct or indirect, that would support Russia's aggression. Mr. President, any unilateral attempt to change the status quo by force is unacceptable anywhere in the world, and such an attempt should never be rewarded. The repercussions of allowing such attempts to occur would be global and undoubtedly affect everyone for years to come. Japan reiterates that this is not a matter of choosing sides between Ukraine and Russia, but of a matter of principle of either upholding or disregarding the UN Charter. Japan will continue its diplomatic efforts and stand firmly with Ukraine. and the international community until comprehensive, just, and last peace, based on the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, is achieved in Ukraine. I thank you.
